summary: Defines how to compute a digest (hash) of an XML document so that the result depends on its content and structure, not on surface differences in how the text is written. Two XML documents that mean the same thing then produce the same hash. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: DOMHASH calculates a digest from an XML document's tree structure instead of from the exact bytes used to write it. This can make equivalent structures produce the same digest despite differences such as namespace prefixes.

questions: why is namespace expansion important in domhash
subtitle: A repeatable way to hash an XML document from its DOM structure.

tldr.problem: The same XML structure can be written as different byte strings, so hashing the serialized text can produce different results for equivalent structures.
tldr.mechanism: DOMHASH defines digests for five DOM node types and builds parent digests from child digests. It uses expanded namespace names and UTF-16BE strings, while omitting comments and document-type nodes.
tldr.outcome: The method provides a specific digest calculation for XML structures and can support signatures or comparisons of changing document trees. It is an Informational memo.

today: RFC 2803 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Hash the Document Tree
sections.content:
XML can represent the same internal document structure with different whitespace, character encodings, entity references or namespace prefixes. If a digest is computed from the serialized text, those surface differences can make two equivalent documents appear different.

RFC 2803 defines DOMHASH as a digest calculation over a Document Object Model (DOM) tree. It describes uses such as XML digital signatures and comparing a cached tree with an updated one.
sections.plainLanguage: Two XML files can look different as text but have the same structure. DOMHASH checks the structure so those writing differences do not change the result.

sections.title: Which Nodes Affect the Digest
sections.content:
DOMHASH defines digests for Text, ProcessingInstruction, Attr, Element and Document nodes. Comment nodes and Document Type nodes do not contribute. Entity references must be expanded before calculation.

Adjacent text nodes are merged, and zero-length text nodes are ignored. Digests are recursive: a parent's digest includes the digests of its parts, so a changed part can be identified without recalculating an unchanged tree from scratch.
sections.plainLanguage: The method includes text, attributes, elements, processing instructions and the document. It ignores comments and type declarations, then combines the parts from the leaves up to the document.

sections.title: How Node Digests Are Calculated
sections.content:
Each node's input to the chosen hash algorithm begins with a four-byte node-type value. Text data and names are encoded as UTF-16BE. A processing instruction includes its target, a two-byte separator and its data; an attribute includes its expanded name, a separator and its value.

An element includes its expanded name, its non-namespace attributes sorted by expanded name, and child digests in order. A document includes its eligible child digests in order. Namespace declaration attributes have no digest.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of node has a fixed recipe for the bytes to hash. An element's recipe includes its name, sorted attributes and children in their original order.

sections.title: Namespaces and Security
sections.content:
DOMHASH uses expanded names so that two different namespace prefixes bound to the same namespace URI do not change the digest. The namespace URI and local name are used instead of the prefix.

The memo says that suitability for digital signatures and integrity uses depends on the selected hash algorithm and on whether the digest includes the parts of the DOM that matter to the application. The digest definition alone does not make a weak hash algorithm secure.
sections.plainLanguage: A namespace prefix is only a local label. DOMHASH uses the namespace's actual name, and the security of the result still depends on the hash algorithm chosen.
